tagline: A winding mountain crossing shaped by a choice of alignment
intro: Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses Glacier National Park in Montana, climbing over the Continental Divide at Logan Pass. Its two lanes are narrow and winding, with hairpin turns especially west of the pass. The road is a National Historic Landmark and a Historic Civil Engineering Landmark. Travel through the central park once took several days; the road made it a journey of a few hours, excluding stops for sightseeing or construction.

Conceived for automobile tourists, it was among the first National Park Service projects intended specifically for that form of travel. Superintendent George Goodwin conceived the road in 1917, and construction began in 1921. National Park Service director Stephen Mather favored landscape architect Thomas Chalmers Vint's alternative route along the Garden Wall. That alignment reduced switchbacks and visual impact but cost more. After Goodwin resigned, Vint's proposal prevailed, and the whole road opened in 1933.

Start at U.S. Route 2 in West Glacier. The road follows Lake McDonald's southern shore before passing the Garden Wall and Weeping Wall on the way to Logan Pass. At 6,646 feet, the pass is the road's highest point. Beyond it, the eastbound route passes Saint Mary Lake and ends at U.S. Route 89 in St. Mary.

moments.title: Lake McDonald
moments.text: Lake McDonald fills a valley shaped by erosion and glacial activity. Glacier National Park's largest lake is approximately ten miles long, with Going-to-the-Sun Road following its southern shoreline. Dense coniferous forest surrounds the water, with spruce, fir and larch among its dominant trees. The lake also marked an earlier way of arriving: Lake McDonald Lodge faces the water, where its early visitors came ashore. Road access arrived by 1921, bringing travelers to what had been the back of the hotel. That entrance retains its secondary character even as it receives road traffic.

moments.title: Weeping Wall
moments.text: The Weeping Wall is a natural waterfall beside Going-to-the-Sun Road. Snowmelt feeds water that seeps from the side of Haystack Butte and the Garden Wall. Haystack Butte rises above it, while the road traverses the peak's western and southern slopes. The peak is visible from both the road and Logan Pass.

moments.title: Logan Pass
moments.text: At Logan Pass, the road reaches 6,646 feet and crosses the Continental Divide. The visitor center at the summit belongs to a later chapter of park travel: the National Park Service's Mission 66 facilities program. Completed in 1966, it uses native stone, glued laminated timber and a broad, gently sloping roof. Its two main levels step up the hillside. The building replaced a simpler summit arrangement: a rest stop with toilets. The design was reduced in size because visitor facilities at St. Mary and West Glacier offered orientation in less demanding surroundings.

practical: Logan Pass: Logan Pass closes in winter because of avalanche hazards. Between Avalanche Creek and Rising Sun picnic areas, vehicles must be no longer than 21 feet and no wider than 8 feet. (checked 2026-10-11)
